Abstract
A compressed self-index stores a string in compressed form while supporting locate queries without de-
compression. For highly repetitive strings—arising in web crawls, versioned documents, and genomic
collections—static self-indexes can match the δ-optimal lower bound of Ω(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n)
bits up to constant factors, where n is the string length, σ is the alphabet size, and δ is the sub-
string complexity. Their dynamic counterparts, however, remain scarce: every existing dynamic
self-index either fails to attain δ-optimal space, pays at least Θ(log n) time per reported occurrence
during locate, or exposes the longest common prefix (LCP) of the text inside its update time. We
present the dynamic RR-index, a dynamic grammar-compressed self-index built on the restricted
recompression run-length straight-line program (RLSLP). To our knowledge, it is the first dynamic
self-index to attain δ-optimal space. The index occupies expected O(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n)
bits, answers locate queries in expected O(m + log m log2 n + occ(log n/ log log n)) time—where m
is the pattern length and occ is the number of occurrences—and supports insertions and deletions
of a length-m′ substring in expected amortized O(m′ log2 n + log3 n) time, with no dependence on
the LCP. On eleven highly repetitive corpora, including a 37 GB Wikipedia dump and a 59 GB
human-chromosome collection, the dynamic RR-index is up to 77× faster than the dynamic r-index
on updates and up to 11× faster than other dynamic indexes on locate.

Introduction
Datasets composed of highly repetitive strings—those with many repeated substrings—have
grown rapidly in recent years. Typical examples include web pages collected by crawlers [14],
version-controlled documents such as Wikipedia with its complete edit history [46], and,
perhaps most notably, biological sequences such as collections of human genomes [42, 45].
These datasets are not static: edits, deletions, and new releases arrive continuously. Yet the
methods practitioners rely on most heavily, such as the r-index [15], a compressed index
supporting locate queries, are static: reflecting even a single edit requires rebuilding the index
from scratch. There is therefore a strong and growing need to develop dynamic compressed
self-indexes for highly repetitive strings, which can be updated efficiently without rebuilding.
A practical solution must simultaneously (i) use space proportional to the repetitiveness
of the string, (ii) answer locate queries quickly, and (iii) support string insertions and
deletions without rebuilding. The third requirement has proven difficult: while compressed
self-indexes—data structures that represent the string in compressed form while answering
locate queries directly—are well understood in the static case, their dynamic counterparts
remain challenging to develop.
For highly repetitive strings, compressed self-indexes aim to approach the δ-optimal
space of O(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n) bits established by Kociumaka et al. [27], where n

is the string length, σ is the alphabet size, and δ is the substring complexity of the string—
a repetitiveness measure satisfying δ ≪n on genomic and versioned corpora. A line of
specialized self-indexes—grammar-based [8, 27, 26], LZ-based [7], block-tree–based [2, 29, 27],
and run-length BWT (RLBWT)–based such as the r-index [15] and OptBWTR [36, 3]—has
closed much of this gap, with several attaining δ-optimal space up to constant factors. None,
however, supports updates.
Only a handful of dynamic self-indexes have been proposed, and each sacrifices at least
one of the three requirements (Table 1 in Appendix A gives the full comparison). The
dynamic FM-index [44, 31] extends the Burrows–Wheeler Transform (BWT) [5] but uses
O(n log σ) bits, oblivious to repetitiveness, with an O(log2+ϵ n) per-occurrence locate factor.
Grammar-based dynamic indexes—the SE-index [35], TST-index-d [40], and Gawrychowski
et al. [16]—either pay (log n log∗n)2-type factors in locate/update or require Ω(n log n) bits.
A recent dynamic r-index [38, 39] uses O(r log n) bits (r the number of BWT runs), but its
update time O((m′ + Lmax) log n) depends on the maximum value Lmax ≤n of the longest
common prefix (LCP) array—the length of the longest repeated substring—which can grow
independently of δ and r as versioned copies accumulate. In short, every existing dynamic
self-index either fails to compress to δ-optimal space, pays at least Θ(log n) time per reported
occurrence during locate, or exposes the LCP inside update time. We address this gap.
Our contributions.
We present the dynamic RR-index, a dynamic grammar-compressed self-
index built on the restricted recompression RLSLP of Jeż [19] and Kociumaka et al. [28, 27].
Our starting observation is that the derivation tree of a restricted recompression admits a com-
pact DAG representation whose explicit-node count is tied to δ rather than to r or g. Moreover,
insertions and deletions perturb this DAG only along two short popped sequences [35, 18], inde-
pendently of the maximum LCP value. Combined with two-dimensional range reporting [4, 33]
and with a path-cached ancestor field that accelerates locate (Section 5.6), this design simul-
taneously achieves δ-optimal space and a sub-logarithmic per-occurrence locate bound. To
our knowledge, the dynamic RR-index is the first dynamic self-index to attain δ-optimal
space. Concretely, it occupies expected δ-optimal space—O(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n)
bits—and answers locate queries in expected O(m + log m log2 n + occ(log n/ log log n)) time,
where m is the pattern length and occ is the number of occurrences. Insertions and deletions
of a length-m′ substring are supported in expected amortized O(m′ log2 n + log3 n) time. We
implement and evaluate the dynamic RR-index on eleven highly repetitive corpora, including
the 37 GB enwiki Wikipedia dump and the 59 GB chr19 genomic collection, and we show that
it is up to 77× faster than the dynamic r-index on updates and up to 11× faster than other
dynamic indexes on locate, while using working memory consistent with scaling by δ. A C++
reference implementation will be released as open-source together with the camera-ready
version.
Organization.
Sections 2–3 fix notation and the structural properties of restricted recom-
pression. Sections 4–5 introduce the dynamic RR-index, its DAG representation, the locate
algorithm, and the ancestor-path caching of Section 5.6. Section 6 gives the insertion and de-

Preliminaries
Basic notation.
Let T be a string of length n ≥2 over a totally ordered alphabet Σ of
size σ = nO(1). Let |T| = n. We denote the empty string by ε, the i-th character of T by
T[i], the substring of T from position i to position j by T[i..j], and the reverse of T by
reverse(T) = T[n], T[n −1], . . . , T[1]. A prefix (resp. suffix) of T is a substring beginning at
position 1 (resp. ending at position n); for a string P ∈Σ+, T · P denotes concatenation.
We use the standard lexicographic order on Σ∗. The set of occurrence positions of P in T
is Occ(T, P) = {i ∈{1, . . . , n −|P| + 1} | T[i..i + |P| −1] = P}. For a nonempty set S of
integers, min S and max S denote its minimum and maximum. For a path P in a graph, let
|P| denote the number of edges on P.
Model of computation.
We will use base-2 logarithms throughout this paper unless
otherwise indicated. Our computation model is a unit-cost word RAM [17] with multiplication,
randomization, and machine word size B = Θ(log n) bits. We measure space in machine
words; multiplying by B gives the space in bits. We analyze our randomized algorithms
against an oblivious adversary [6]: the sequence of updates to T is chosen in advance, without
access to the random bits used by our algorithms.
Substring complexity.
Substring complexity [43, 8] measures the repetitiveness of a string.
For each d ≥1, let Sd = {T[i..i + d −1] | 1 ≤i ≤n −d + 1} be the set of length-d substrings
of T. The substring complexity of T is δ = max1≤d≤n |Sd|/d.
The δ-optimal space is Θ(δ log n log σ
δ log n log n) bits: every string can be encoded in the bits,
and this bound is tight in n, σ, and δ [27].
Grammar-based compression.
A grammar-based compression of T is a context-free gram-
mar G = (V, Σ, D, E) that generates exactly T, where V = {X1, X2, . . . , Xg} is a set of
nonterminals, Σ is the alphabet of T, and D is a set of production rules Xi →expri with
expri ∈(V ∪Σ)∗. A rule Xi →expri expands Xi to the sequence expri. The start symbol
E ∈V does not appear on any right-hand side, while every other nonterminal does appear
on at least one. To avoid cycles, we require j < i whenever Xj appears in expri. In addition,
expri ̸= exprj for two distinct integers i, j ∈{1, 2, . . . , g}.
Each nonterminal X ∈V derives a substring of T; in particular, the start symbol E
derives T itself. The tree whose root is labeled E and whose leaves spell out T is the
derivation tree of G. Let val(X) denote the substring of T derived by X ∈V, and let
val(X1, X2, . . . , Xd) = val(X1) · val(X2) · . . . · val(Xd) for nonterminals X1, X2, . . . , Xd ∈V.
A straight-line program (SLP) [20] is a grammar-based compression in which each nonter-
minal produces either a character or a pair of nonterminals. A run-length SLP (RLSLP) [34]
is an SLP whose nonterminals can additionally produce a repetition of a single nonterminal.
Specifically, D ⊆V × (Σ ∪V+), and each production rule in D takes one of the following
forms: (i) Xi →c for c ∈Σ; (ii) Xi →XjXk (j, k < i) for distinct nonterminals Xj, Xk ∈V;
(iii) Xi →Xj (j < i) for Xj ∈V; (iv) Xi →(Xj)d (j < i), where (Xj)d denotes d ≥2
successive copies of Xj ∈V. Several algorithms build an RLSLP for a given string, e.g.,
signature encoding [34], recompression [19], signature grammar [7], and restricted block
compression [26].

Restricted Recompression
Restricted recompression [27, 28] is a randomized algorithm that constructs an RLSLP
GR whose derivation tree is height-balanced (i.e., all children of every node have the same
height). Let H denote the height of the derivation tree of GR. For each h ∈{0, 1, . . . , H},
the nonterminals labeling the nodes at height h, read left to right, form a sequence Sh. In
this paper, GR is called restricted recompression RLSLP.
Restricted recompression builds the derivation tree bottom-up, processing S0, S1, . . . , SH
in order. While processing Sh, each newly introduced nonterminal Xi is assigned a value
assign(Xi) ∈{−1, 0, 1} as follows.
Let µ(h) = (8/7)⌈h/2⌉−1.
If |val(Xi)| ≤µ(h), then
assign(Xi) is drawn uniformly at random from {0, 1}; otherwise, assign(Xi) = −1. The assign
values partition Sh into segments. Each segment is one of the following: (i) a maximal
run of the same nonterminal Xi with assign(Xi) ∈{0, 1}; (ii) two distinct nonterminals
Xi and Xj with assign(Xi) = 1 and assign(Xj) = 0; or (iii) a single nonterminal Xi with
assign(Xi) ∈{−1, 0, 1}.
Figure 1 shows an example of the derivation tree for T = abaaacbaaa. Since the actual
values of µ(h) would make the tree too large to display, we use ⌊µ(0)⌋= ⌊µ(1)⌋= 1 and
⌊µ(2)⌋= ⌊µ(3)⌋= · · · = ⌊µ(8)⌋= 10 in the figure.

4
Dynamic RR-index
The dynamic RR-index is built on the restricted recompression RLSLP GR = (V, Σ, D, E)
introduced in the previous section. It consists of two components: (i) a directed acyclic
graph (DAG) representing the derivation tree, and (ii) a set of points in two-dimensional
space corresponding to explicit nodes in the DAG. The details of these two components are
described in the following subsection.
4.1
DAG Representation of Derivation Tree and Path Decomposition
DAG representation.
The derivation tree of GR is represented as a directed acyclic mul-
tigraph [34, 35] D = (U, E, src, dst, LU, LE) obtained by merging nodes labeled with the
same nonterminal: LU : U →V is a bijection between nodes and nonterminals, E is the
set of directed edges; for e ∈E, src(e) is its source (corresponding to a parent node in the
derivation tree) and dst(e) its destination (a child node), and the outgoing edges of ui are
in one-to-one correspondence with those of any node labeled LU(ui) in the derivation tree.
The label LE(e) ∈{0, 1, . . . , n −1} is j −i, where i and j are the starting positions of the
substrings derived from src(e) and dst(e). Let d+(u) denote the outdegree of u. Figure 2
(left) illustrates this for Figure 1.

4.2
Point Representation of Explicit Nodes
To support efficient locate queries, we map each explicit node ui ∈Uexpl to a point pi in two-
dimensional space at x-coordinate Li and y-coordinate Ri, defined from the production rule
of Xi = LU(ui) as follows: if Xi →XjXk then Li = reverse(val(Xj)) and Ri = val(Xk); if
Xi →c for c ∈Σ then Li = c and Ri = ε; if Xi →(Xj)d with d ≥2 then Li = reverse(val(Xj))
and Ri = val((Xj)d−1). Let P be the resulting point set, and let X and Y be Uexpl sorted
lexicographically by Li and Ri, with ties broken by ui. This point representation will later
allow us to find the relevant explicit nodes for locate queries by two-dimensional range
reporting, i.e., by queries that return all points in a given axis-aligned rectangle. Figure 3
illustrates P, X, and Y for the DAG in Figure 2.
4.3
Dynamic Data Structures for the DAG and Point Set
The DAG D is indexed by DDAG(Π) and the point set P by Dgrid(P).

Data structure for path decomposition.
DDAG(Π) consists of a doubly linked list and two
types of hash tables [11]. Intra-path edges are implicit in the list structure; inter-path edges
are stored in per-path hash tables. For each explicit node u ∈Uexpl with Xi := LU(u), the list
stores one element associated with the endpoint u that records: a pair (u, |Pu|) for recovering
Pu, the production rule Xi →expri, the height of u, |val(Xi)|, and assign(LU(uj)) for each
node uj on Pu (occupying O(H) bits since |Pu| ≤H + 1 and each label is 2 bits). For each
path Pu ∈Π, the set Eexpl(Pu) = {e ∈E | src(e) ∈Uexpl, dst(e) lies on Pu} is indexed by a
per-path hash table whose entry for e has key src(e) and value dst(e) (only distinct key-value
pairs are stored); the keys are also linked in a doubly linked list sorted by the height of the
corresponding nodes and indexed by a list indexing data structure [9]. A global hash table
indexes the M production rules with key expri (encoded in O(B) bits) and value Xi.
Data structure for point set.
We index P ⊆X × Y by Blelloch’s dynamic data structure
Dgrid(P) [4] for range reporting and point insertion/deletion, which requires O(1)-time
comparison of elements of X and Y. We maintain order maintenance data structures [10]
on X and Y to provide O(1)-time comparison and O(log M)-time insertion/deletion, and
list indexing data structures for O(log M)-time access; each coordinate is a pointer to the
corresponding list element of Π, so each point uses O(B) bits. Each list element of DDAG(Π)
in turn stores pointers into the list indexing and order maintenance structures for X and Y.
Range reporting takes O(log M + rocc(log M/ log log M)) time where rocc is the number of
reported points, and a point insertion or deletion takes amortized O(log M) time.
4.4
Space Complexity
The doubly linked list contributes O(M(H + B)) bits; the global hash table, the per-path
hash tables (which hold O(M) distinct key-value pairs in total since every DAG node has
at most two children) together with their list indexing structures, and Dgrid(P) with its
auxiliary structures each contribute O(MB) bits. Summing, the dynamic RR-index occupies
O(M(H + B)) bits. Since B = Θ(log n) and E[M] = O(δ log n log σ
δ log n ), the total space is
δ-optimal in expectation under the assumption that H = O(log n).
5
Locate Query Algorithm
This section presents the algorithm answering a locate query for a pattern P of length m,
establishing the baseline complexity bound (Theorem 5); Section 5.6 then improves the
per-occurrence factor to log n/ log log n via ancestor-path caching (Theorem 6). For m ≥2,
the algorithm proceeds in four steps, each detailed in a subsection below: from the derivation
tree we extract a specific core [32] of P as the popped sequence [12, 18] of ρ runs, build ρ
axis-aligned rectangles in P, apply range reporting to obtain the primary occurrences [35],
and convert these into Occ(T, P) by traversing the DAG to the root. The case m = 1 is
handled separately in Section 5.5.
5.1
Step (i): Computing the Popped Sequence
This step computes the popped sequence of P, a specific core of P whose run-length encoding
has O(min{m, H}) runs. We first introduce what a core is, and then introduce the popped
sequence as a specific construction.
Let Q = X1, X2, . . . , Xd be a sequence of nonterminals (each Xi ∈V) such that val(Q) =
P. We say that Q is embedded in the derivation tree of GR at position s ∈{1, 2, . . . , n} if,

Since a core of P is not unique, we use a specific one called the popped sequence of

5.2
Step (ii): Computing the Rectangles from the Popped Sequence
Primary occurrences and their rectangles.
A primary occurrence [35] of P for a split
position ℓ∈{1, 2, . . . , m −1} is a pair (ui, ℓ) with ui ∈Uexpl such that (i) reverse(P[1..ℓ]) is
a prefix of Li and (ii) P[ℓ+ 1..m] is a prefix of Ri; that is, ui is an explicit node where an
occurrence of P crosses the first boundary between substrings derived from ui’s production
rule. We write pOcc(P, ℓ) ⊆Uexpl for the set of such ui at split position ℓ. Recall from
Section 4.2 that ui is mapped to the point pi with x-coordinate Li and y-coordinate Ri.
The two prefix conditions constrain Li and Ri, respectively, so pOcc(P, ℓ) coincides with the
set of points of P in the axis-aligned rectangle rectℓ= [x, x′] × [y, y′], where x, x′ ∈X are
the smallest and largest elements whose x-coordinate has reverse(P[1..ℓ]) as a prefix, and
y, y′ ∈Y are the analogous bounds for P[ℓ+ 1..m] (if any of the four does not exist, rectℓis
empty).
Reducing to ρ rectangles.
Because the popped sequence is a core of P, only split positions
at its run boundaries can yield a nonempty pOcc(P, ℓ), as formalized below.
▶Lemma 2 (Generalization of Lemma 7 in [35]). Let Q be a core of a pattern P of length

Update Operations
6.1
Insertion Operation
Given a string P ′ ∈Σ+ of length m′ = O(n) and a position s ∈{1, 2, . . . , n}, the insertion
operation produces T ′ by inserting P ′ into T at position s and updates the dynamic RR-index
so that its RLSLP derives T ′. For simplicity, we focus on 2 ≤s ≤n −1, so that T ′ is
the concatenation of T[1..s −1], P ′, and T[s..n]; the boundary cases s = 1 and s = n
are analogous.
Following the standard strategy of dynamic grammar-compressed data
structures [40, 35, 37, 34], the update proceeds in three phases (see Appendix D for details).
Phase 1: constructing the derivation tree of GR′.
The first phase constructs the derivation
tree of an RLSLP GR′ = (V′, Σ′, D′, E′) deriving T ′ by restricted recompression, computing
(H′+1) sequences S′0, S′1, . . . , S′H′ bottom-up; production rules are shared with GR whenever
the right-hand sides agree. For each nonterminal in GR′ \ GR, we insert the corresponding
node into the DAG and update the dynamic data structures.
A naive construction is
Ω(n + m′) since the tree has n + m′ leaves. We reduce this cost using the popped sequences
QL and QR of T[1..s −1] and T[s..n]: since each popped sequence is a core of its source,
QL and QR are embedded in the derivation tree of GR′ at positions 1 and s + m′ as
subtrees that need not be reconstructed. Concretely, (i) compute QL and QR by [12] in
O(H) time; (ii) build S′0, . . . , S′H′ in O(|Tdiff|) time, where Tdiff collects (A) the ancestors
of the embedded subtree roots, (B) the m′ leaves on T ′[s..s + m′ −1], and (C) their
ancestors. Figure 5 illustrates the embeddings. The phase runs in expected amortized
O(|Tdiff| + |Iexpl| max{H, H′, log M} log M + |Iimpl|) time, where Iexpl (resp. Iimpl) is the set
of explicit (resp. implicit) nodes inserted into the DAG; see Appendix D.1.
Phase 2: removing obsolete nonterminals.
For each nonterminal in GR \ GR′, remove the
corresponding node from the DAG and update the dynamic data structures. This phase takes
expected amortized O(|Rexpl| log M + |Rimpl|) time; see Appendix D.2 for details. Here, Rexpl
(respectively, Rimpl) is the set of explicit (respectively, implicit) nodes whose nonterminals do
not appear in the derivation tree of GR′.
Phase 3: updating ancestor-path caches and coordinate prefixes.
For each explicit node
in Iexpl ∪Uchange, update the additional information stored in the corresponding element of the
doubly linked list for Π. Here, Uchange ⊆Uexpl is the set of explicit nodes that have an ancestor
in Iexpl∪Iimpl∪Rexpl∪Rimpl within distance ⌈α+log B⌉in the DAG. This phase takes O(Wmax+
(|Uchange| + |Iexpl|)(H′ + B)) time, where Wmax = max{|Iexpl|, |Iimpl|, |Rexpl|, |Rimpl|, |Uchange|};
see Appendix D.3 for details.

Construction Algorithm
Restricted recompression proceeds as follows. At level 0, for each position s ∈[1, n], the
algorithm introduces a fresh nonterminal Xis with rule Xis →T[s] and determines assign(Xis).
The sequence S0 is then Xi1, Xi2, . . . , Xin. Here, for two characters T[s] and T[s′], Xis = Xis′
if and only if T[s] = T[s′].
For each h ≥1, Sh is built from Sh−1 in two steps. In the first step, Sh−1 is decomposed
into segments F1, F2, . . . left-to-right as follows. Suppose Sh−1[1..s −1] has been decomposed
into F1, . . . , Fj−1; then the next segment Fj, starting at position s, is:
1. Fj = Sh−1[s..s + 1] if h is even, assign(Sh−1[s]) = 1, and assign(Sh−1[s + 1]) = 0;
2. Fj = Sh−1[s..s + ℓ−1], the longest run of Sh−1[s] starting at position s, if h is odd and
assign(Sh−1[s]) ̸= −1;
3. Fj = Sh−1[s] otherwise.
In the second step, for each segment Fj of Sh−1, the algorithm introduces a fresh
nonterminal Xij with rule Xij →Fj and determines assign(Xij). Concatenating these
nonterminals in order yields Sh. Here, for two segments Fj and Fj′, Xij = Xij′ if and only
if Fj = Fj′.
These two steps are applied for h = 1, 2, . . . until the sequence has length one; the final
sequence is SH, with H ≥1 since |S0| = n ≥2.
The algorithm outputs an RLSLP GR = (V, Σ, D, E), where V collects the nonterminals
introduced across S0, S1, . . . , SH; Σ is the alphabet of T; D is the set of production rules
created above; and the start symbol E is the unique nonterminal in SH.
By Corollary V.11 of [27], the algorithm terminates with probability 1, and its expected
running time is O(n).

at the last node of P. If the last node of P is not a leaf, then the subtree rooted at that
node is recursively decomposed into paths.

D.1
Details of Phase 1
Update of dynamic RR-index.
Every time a new production rule Xi →expri is established,
a new node ui of height h corresponding to Xi is inserted into the DAG. If ui is explicit,
then a new path P = ui is inserted into Π, and a new directed edge e from ui to the node uj
corresponding to each nonterminal Xj in expri is inserted into Eexpl(Pj), where Pj ∈Π is the
path containing uj.
Otherwise (i.e., ui is implicit), expri consists of a single nonterminal Xj′, the corresponding
node uj′ is the first node of a path P′ ∈Π, and the path is extended by connecting ui and P′.
To reflect the changes of Π and Eexpl(Pj), we need to update the following data structures:
The global hash table. If ui is explicit, Xi and the binary representation of expri are inserted
into the hash table as a value and its key, respectively. This insertion takes expected
amortized O(1) time [11].
The list element corresponding to P. If ui is explicit, then create a new element corres-
ponding to P, append it to the doubly linked list for Π, and associate an empty hash
table with it. This element stores the following five pieces of information: (i) a pair (ui, 0)
for recovering P from the element, (ii) expri, (iii) h, (iv) |val(Xi)|, and (v) assign(Xi).
Here, |val(Xi)| is computed by summing up the length of the substring derived from each
nonterminal Xj in expri if expri is a sequence of nonterminals. Otherwise, |val(Xi)| = 1.
|val(Xi)| can be computed in O(1) time using Lemma 4. Therefore, the list element can
be updated in O(1) time.
The list element corresponding to P′. If ui is implicit, then the second component of the
pair stored in the list element is increased by one, and assign(Xi) is appended to the list
element. These updates take O(max{1, h/B}) time.
The per-path hash table corresponding to Pj. The key and value of the directed edge e
are inserted into the hash table if the hash table does not have the key. This insertion
takes expected amortized O(1) time. In addition, the key of e is inserted into the doubly
linked list for the keys at an appropriate position. The list indexing data structure can
support a random access to the keys and an insertion into the list in O(log M) time [9].
To compute the appropriate insertion position, we need O(log M) random accesses to the
keys. Therefore, the update of the doubly linked list takes O(log2 M) time in total.
The dynamic data structures for X. If ui is explicit, then Li is inserted after the largest
element in X preceding the x-coordinate Li of ui, and the list indexing and order
maintenance data structures for X are updated accordingly in O(log M) time. The
largest element is found by a binary search on X in O(max{H, H′, log M} log M) time,
using the same approach as in the locate query algorithm.
The dynamic data structures for Y. Similar to the update of the dynamic data structures
for X, Ri is inserted after the largest element in Y preceding the y-coordinate Ri of ui,

and the list indexing data structure and order maintenance data structure corresponding
to Y are updated accordingly. This update takes O(max{H, H′, log M} log M) time.
The dynamic data structures for P. If ui is explicit, then the corresponding point is in-
serted into P, and the dynamic data structure for range reporting queries is updated
accordingly in amortized O(log M) time.
These updates take amortized O(max{H, H′, log M} log M) time if ui is explicit; other-

Algorithm.
The first phase consists of the following two steps.
(i) Compute QL and QR using the algorithm of [12]. This is done by traversing the derivation
tree of GR from the root to the nodes corresponding to the sequence QL embedded at
position 1 and the sequence QR embedded at position s, respectively. By Lemma 4, these
traversals can be performed in O(H) time.
(ii) Compute Tdiff in O(|Tdiff|) time using the rule query introduced in Appendix C.5. This
computation may create new production rules. Whenever a new production rule Xi →
expri is established, we update the dynamic RR-index accordingly.
Therefore, the expected amortized running time of the first phase is
O(|Tdiff| + |Iexpl| max{H, H′, log M} log M + |Iimpl|),
where Iexpl and Iimpl are introduced in Section 6.
D.2
Details of Phase 2
Computation of Rexpl ∪Rimpl.
To update the dynamic RR-index, we need to identify the
nodes in Rexpl ∪Rimpl. For this purpose, we use the following observation: a node ui belongs
to Rexpl ∪Rimpl if and only if all parents of ui belong to Rexpl ∪Rimpl.
We start from the node ui corresponding to the start symbol E of GR, letting P ∈Π
denote the path containing ui; this ui has an incoming edge only if E still appears in GR′.
Rexpl ∪Rimpl can be computed recursively as follows:
(i) Determine whether ui has an incoming edge. This can be verified in O(1) time: ui has at
least one incoming edge if (A) ui is not the first node of P, or (B) ui is the first node of
P and one incoming edge of ui is explicitly stored in the list element corresponding to P.
(ii) If ui has an incoming edge, then the recursion stops. Otherwise, ui belongs to Rexpl∪Rimpl;
we output ui, remove ui and its outgoing edges from the DAG, and recursively process
the target node of each outgoing edge of ui that has not yet been removed.
By the observation above, this recursive algorithm correctly computes Rexpl ∪Rimpl. Since
it processes O(|Rexpl| + |Rimpl|) nodes, its running time is O(|Rexpl| + |Rimpl|). This bound
excludes the update time of the dynamic RR-index.
Update of dynamic RR-index.
Whenever a node is removed from the DAG, the dynamic
RR-index is updated accordingly. As in Phase 1, this update takes expected amortized
O(log M) time if the removed node is explicit, and O(1) time otherwise. Therefore, Phase 2
takes expected amortized O(|Rexpl| log M + |Rimpl|) time in total.

To compute Uchange, we introduce a set Uchildren ⊆U of nodes u satisfying the following two
conditions: (i) a parent of u is removed from or inserted into the DAG when updating the
RLSLP GR (i.e., u is a child of a node in Iexpl ∪Iimpl ∪Rexpl ∪Rimpl); and (ii) u itself is neither

can be computed in O(|Rexpl| + |Rimpl| + |Iexpl| + |Iimpl|) time by modifying the algorithm for
computing Rexpl ∪Rimpl. Here, |Rexpl| + |Rimpl| + |Iexpl| + |Iimpl| = O(Wmax).
Computation of Uchange.
Let u ∈Uexpl be an explicit node that is neither inserted into nor
removed from the DAG when updating the RLSLP GR. Then, u ∈Uchange if and only if either
u ∈Uchildren or u is a descendant of a node in Uchildren within distance ⌈α + log B⌉−1. Hence,
analogously to the algorithm for Rexpl ∪Rimpl, Uchange is computed by traversing the DAG
from the nodes in Uchildren. This traversal takes O(|Uchange|) time, where |Uchange| ≤Wmax.
Recomputation of the first ⌈βB/ log σ⌉characters in Li and Ri.
For each node ui, the
first ⌈βB/ log σ⌉characters of Li and of Ri are each obtained by a random access query in

We start with a path Q consisting only of ui and extend it to
PvOcc(ui) by a recursive algorithm. The algorithm traverses the DAG from ui to the root.
Suppose that Q has already been extended to the last node ui1 of a path P = uid →uid−1 →
· · · →ui1 in Π. Let η be the number of keys stored in the per-path hash table for Eexpl(P).
For each integer x ∈{1, 2, . . . , η}, let ex ∈Eexpl(P) be an inter-path edge corresponding to
the x-th key src(ex) in the doubly linked list for the η keys, and let zx be the number of
directed edges from src(ex) to dst(ex).
The recursive algorithm consists of seven steps.
The first step computes z1, zη−1, and zη. Each zx is computed in O(1) time using
Lemma 4(ii) and the corresponding key-value pair (src(ex), dst(ex)). The three keys src(e1),
src(eη−1), and src(eη) can be accessed in O(1) time via the doubly linked list, and their
values via the per-path hash table. Therefore, the first step takes O(1) time.
The second step verifies whether |Eexpl(P)| = 0. This takes O(1) time, because |Eexpl(P)| = 0
if and only if η = 0.
The third step verifies whether |Eexpl(P)| = 1.
This also takes O(1) time, because
|Eexpl(P)| = 1 if and only if η = 1 and z1 = 1.
The fourth step verifies whether |Eexpl(P)| ≥2. This takes O(1) time, because |Eexpl(P)| ≥2

Abstract: A compressed self-index stores a string in compressed form while supporting locate queries without de- compression. For highly repetitive strings—arising in web crawls, versioned documents, and genomic collections—static self-indexes can match the δ-optimal lower bound of Ω(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n) bits up to constant factors, where n is the string length, σ is the alphabet size, and δ is the sub- string complexity. Their dynamic counterparts, however, remain scarce: every existing dynamic self-index either fails to attain δ-optimal space, pays at least Θ(log n) time per reported occurrence during locate, or exposes the longest common prefix (LCP) of the text inside its update time. We present the dynamic RR-index, a dynamic grammar-compressed self-index built on the restricted recompression run-length straight-line program (RLSLP). To our knowledge, it is the first dynamic self-index to attain δ-optimal space. The index occupies expected O(δ log(n log σ/(δ log n)) log n) bits, answers locate queries in expected O(m + log m log2 n + occ(log n/ log log n)) time—where m is the pattern length and occ is the number of occurrences—and supports insertions and deletions of a length-m′ substring in expected amortized O(m′ log2 n + log3 n) time, with no dependence on the LCP. On eleven highly repetitive corpora, including a 37 GB Wikipedia dump and a 59 GB human-chromosome collection, the dynamic RR-index is up to 77× faster than the dynamic r-index on updates and up to 11× faster than other dynamic indexes on locate. 2012 ACM Subject Classification Theory of computation →Pattern matching
